structured_extraction.program_description: The CLIF Program distributes casino gaming tax revenues from electronic slot machines at the Horseshoe Casino to benefit communities in immediate proximity to the casino in South Baltimore. Funds are allocated to support infrastructure investments, facilities, public safety, sanitation, economic and community development including housing, and other public services and investments aligned with the South Baltimore Gateway Master Plan. The Baltimore Casino Local Development Council advises the City on developing multi-year and annual spending plans for these funds. The South Baltimore Casino Impact District Management Authority (operating as South Baltimore Gateway Partnership) receives fifty percent of the designated funds and operates under an independent Board of Directors.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Annual grants and subsidies allocated through spending plans developed in consultation with the Local Development Council, City agencies, community partners, and neighborhood associations. Funds are distributed according to nine Master Plan goals: Transportation Connectivity, Environmental Sustainability, Safety, Community Development and Revitalization, Economic Growth, Education, Health and Wellness, Quality of Life, and Infrastructure. Casino Local Impact Grant funds are tax revenues from video lottery terminals allocated to Baltimore City for services and improvements in South Baltimore communities near the casino.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Communities in immediate proximity to the casino in South Baltimore, including residents, businesses, organizations, and institutions serving the designated geographic area.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Infrastructure investments, facilities, public safety, sanitation, economic and community development including housing, and other public services and improvements aligned with the South Baltimore Gateway Master Plan goals.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City - The South Baltimore Gateway, a geographic area centered on the Horseshoe Casino in South Baltimore, as defined by state law and shown on the program map. Specifically, communities in immediate proximity to the casino located in South Baltimore, Baltimore City.
requirements_list: Projects must align with the nine South Baltimore Gateway Master Plan goals
Projects must benefit the South Baltimore Gateway area
Located in communities in immediate proximity to the casino in South Baltimore
Funding decisions are made by the Mayor and City Council as part of the City budget approval process
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Annual and multi-year spending plans are developed through consultation between the Baltimore City Department of Planning, Local Development Council members, City agencies, community partners, and neighborhood associations. The LDC has 45 days to review, comment, and make recommendations on the plan. The City makes best efforts to accommodate the recommendations of the LDC before adopting the plan. Specific project proposals are considered through the annual budget process.

structured_extraction.program_description: An out-of-school job training program providing CNA/GNA (Certified Nursing Assistant/Geriatric Nursing Assistant) and automotive technician certifications for young adults.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: The program provides CNA/GNA (Certified Nursing Assistant/Geriatric Nursing Assistant) and automotive technician certifications.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Baltimore City residents aged 18 to 24 with a high school diploma or G.E.D.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: CNA/GNA and automotive technician certifications
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City
requirements_list: Must be a Baltimore City resident
Must be aged 18 to 24
Must have a high school diploma or G.E.D.
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Contact Mark Saunders for application information.

structured_extraction.program_description: Supports students by providing funding for their education and helping them make smart financial decisions regarding their educational pursuits.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Provides scholarships and financial support to help students fund their education.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Students seeking educational funding and financial guidance.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Education expenses including tuition and related costs.
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Contact Central Scholarship directly through phone or email for application details.

structured_extraction.program_name: Certified Historic District for Tax Incentives (National Register)
structured_extraction.program_description: A tax incentive program for property owners in certified historic districts listed on the National Register of Historic Places. Properties in eligible historic districts may qualify for federal and state tax credits for qualified rehabilitation work.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Property owners in the Canton Historic District and other certified historic districts in Baltimore may be eligible for federal and state tax credits for qualified rehabilitation expenses on historic properties.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Property owners with historic properties in certified historic districts in Baltimore City
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Qualified rehabilitation and restoration work on historic properties
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Properties located in the Canton Historic District and other certified historic districts within Baltimore City
requirements_list: Property must be located in a certified historic district listed on the National Register of Historic Places
Work must be qualified rehabilitation meeting historic preservation standards
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Contact Baltimore City Department of Planning for information on tax credit eligibility and application procedures

structured_extraction.program_description: A program that provides funding to build capacity of existing and new child care providers and develops a coordinated workforce pipeline to recruit, train, and place individuals into childcare roles.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: The FY2027 budget includes funding to build capacity of existing and new child care providers, creating an additional 500 quality child care slots in the city. The program develops a coordinated workforce pipeline that leverages existing city, state, and education systems to recruit, train, and place individuals into childcare roles.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Child care providers and individuals seeking training and placement in child care positions in Baltimore City.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Building capacity of child care providers and workforce training and placement.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City

structured_extraction.program_description: A comprehensive program that works to reduce lead poisoning in Baltimore City through primary prevention services, lead testing, home visits and case management, advocacy, and enforcement of the city's lead laws. The program provides preventative home visits to low-income pregnant women and families with children under age 6 to assess lead hazards, conducts Healthy Homes Gatherings for community education, offers point of care blood lead testing, provides case management services to families with lead-poisoned children, and pursues legal action against property owners who fail to abate lead violations.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: The program provides free preventative home visits to assess lead hazards, education and supplies for home environmental health issues, point of care blood lead testing at community health fairs and events, case management services, telephonic or in-person education, referrals to legal and financial resources to address lead hazards, cleaning education, nutrition guidance, and referrals to social and environmental programs. Case management services remain active for at least six months.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Low-income pregnant women and families with children under age 6 living in Baltimore City, with focus on high-risk populations in neighborhoods with high levels of lead-poisoned children. All Baltimore City children ages 1 and 2 are mandated to be tested for lead.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: The program provides education, testing, home visits, case management, and referrals to address lead hazards in homes. Families receive referrals to legal and financial resources to address lead hazards as well as education and supplies for other home environmental health issues.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Limited to Baltimore City.
requirements_list: Children ages 1 and 2 in Baltimore City are mandated by state and Baltimore City Health Code to receive blood lead testing
Families with children who have blood lead levels at 5 ug/dL or above are eligible for outreach and case management
Low-income status for preventative home visits
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Families can contact the Baltimore City Health Department to request preventative home visits. For blood lead testing, contact your physician or the Baltimore Health Care Access hotline at 410-649-0500. Testing labs automatically send results to the Primary Care Provider and to BCHD and MDE if levels are 5 ug/dL or above. Contact is then initiated by BCHD to offer case management services.

structured_extraction.program_description: A community garden program that lets people in Baltimore City rent garden spaces to grow vegetables, herbs, and flowers. The program is open to everyone regardless of gardening experience level. Beginners receive support from experienced gardeners, plus educational resources like lessons and guides. Gardens are located in parks throughout Baltimore City.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Participants pay a one-time $10 non-refundable application fee and a small rental fee based on garden location and plot size. Rental options include a regular-sized bed (10 feet by 15 feet) or a smaller raised bed (9 feet by 6 feet). Amenities included are fenced and locked gardens with dawn-to-dusk access via key, city water (April through October), hoses, wheelbarrows, wood chips, and manure during the growing season.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Baltimore City residents and anyone interested in community gardening, regardless of experience level.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Growing vegetables, herbs, and flowers in rented garden plots.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available to residents of Baltimore City at multiple garden locations throughout the city including Carroll Garden, Clifton Garden, Cimaglia Garden, Dewees Garden, Druid Hill Garden, Heath Street at Charles Street Garden, Leakin Garden, Light Street at Heath Street Garden, Patterson Garden, Rockrose Garden, and Roosevelt Garden.
requirements_list: Must sign a City Farms agreement
Pay one-time $10 application fee
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Interested gardeners contact the City Farm Coordinator, pay the $10 application fee, sign the City Farms agreement, and pay the rental fee for their chosen plot size and location.

structured_extraction.program_name: City of Baltimore Lead Hazard Reduction and Healthy Homes Program
structured_extraction.program_description: A multi-year program providing comprehensive lead hazard control measures and healthy homes interventions to assist low to moderate income households with children under age six who have elevated blood lead levels and reside in dwellings constructed before 1978 in Baltimore City. Activities include lead-based paint risk assessments, lead hazard reduction (window replacement, abatement, paint stabilization, dust wipe testing), healthy homes assessments and interventions, outreach and education, and post-remediation home visits.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: HUD grant funding totaling $4,100,000 over 48 months (April 1, 2026 to April 1, 2030), with $3,600,000 allocated to Lead-Based Paint Hazard Control and $500,000 allocated to Healthy Homes Supplemental Program. Activities include: Lead-Based Paint Risk Assessments in 200 units, Lead Hazard Reduction in 100 units, 100 Healthy Homes Housing Rating System assessments, 80 Healthy Homes interventions, 40 outreach and education sessions, 100 post-remediation education home visits, and 200 lead education home visits. Local Match Funds total $1,516,000.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Low to moderate income households with children under age six who have elevated blood lead levels and reside in dwellings constructed prior to 1978 in Baltimore City.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Lead-based paint risk assessments, lead hazard reduction (window replacement, abatement of lead hazards, paint stabilization and dust wipe clearance testing), healthy homes assessments, healthy homes interventions to identify and address environmental and safety hazards, outreach and education sessions, post-remediation education, and lead education with visual inspections and referral information.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Dwellings constructed prior to 1978 in Baltimore City.
requirements_list: Household must be low to moderate income
Must have children under age six
Children must have elevated blood lead levels (EBLL)
Dwelling must be located in Baltimore City
Dwelling must have been constructed prior to 1978
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: The City of Baltimore Department of Housing & Community Development submitted a request to HUD for release of funds. Public comments on the Environmental Review Record were accepted through April 13, 2026. HUD will consider objections to the release of funds for fifteen days following the submission date based on specific criteria outlined in 24 CFR Part 58.

structured_extraction.program_description: Neighborhood beautification competition and grant program taking place summer 2026. Provides up to $1,500 financial support for block-level cleaning and beautification projects. Inspired by the AFRO Clean Block competitions that began in 1934. Supports residents in creating flourishing, healthy, and beautiful neighborhoods.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Up to $1,500 per project for cleaning and beautification initiatives. Up to 20% of funds may be used for refreshments (food/drinks at events). Funds may support stipends for youth, planting events, weekly clean-ups, or community events. Funds can be layered with other funding sources for larger projects. Supplies and technical expertise provided. Organizing support provided.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Baltimore City residents, community organizations and groups, youth and neighborhood leaders, under and unemployed city residents, and community leaders in Baltimore City neighborhoods.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Trash collection and beautification elements (art, plants, lights, seating), supplies for cleaning and beautification projects, stipends for youth participants, planting events, weekly cleanup events, refreshments and incentives for participants (up to 20%), and marketing costs.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City neighborhoods. Priority given to applications within or near Clean Corps service areas (42 neighborhoods across the city as of 2025).
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Complete the interest form and submit for consideration in the competition.

structured_extraction.program_description: A program that funds regional teams of crew members to conduct vacant lot cleaning and mowing services, alley cleaning, tree pit services, and street cleaning throughout Baltimore City neighborhoods.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: The FY2027 budget includes $3 million to fund Clean Corps, which operates twelve regional teams of crew members providing cleaning and maintenance services. Combined with remaining ARPA funds, these dollars support extensive cleanup services across the city.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Baltimore City neighborhoods.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Vacant lot cleaning and mowing, alley cleaning, tree pit services, and street cleaning.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City

structured_extraction.program_description: CollegeBound Foundation encourages and enables Baltimore City public high school students to attend college by providing full-time college advisors, need-based last-dollar grants, college counseling, and comprehensive support services. The foundation delivers financial assistance to help students access higher education after securing other financial aid sources, and works with mixed-status families to identify additional financial aid and scholarships. Services include admission procedure forums, SAT preparation assistance, campus visit coordination, and help completing financial aid forms.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Full-time college advisors provide guidance and comprehensive college counseling support. Need-based last-dollar grants (scholarships) help eligible students pay for college after other financial aid sources are applied, covering remaining tuition costs, SAT fees, and financial aid application fees. Historically, over 608 students have received grants totaling approximately $1.8+ million in assistance.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Baltimore City public high school students, including mixed-status families, who are interested in attending college and meet academic qualifications but lack sufficient financial resources.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: College tuition and related educational expenses, SAT preparation fees, and financial aid application fees. Last-dollar grants fill remaining gap after other financial aid sources have been secured.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Operates in 18 Baltimore City public high schools and serves Baltimore City public high school students only.
requirements_list: Attend a participating Baltimore City public high school
Must be interested in attending college
Must have academic qualifications to attend college
Must lack sufficient family financial resources
Must apply for other financial aid sources first (last-dollar grant fills remaining gap)
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Students work with CollegeBound Foundation full-time college advisors who provide comprehensive assistance including college counseling, support with college selection, help completing financial aid forms, SAT preparation, campus visit coordination, and award last-dollar grants to cover remaining tuition costs. CollegeBound staff conduct forums to familiarize students with admission procedures and the grant application process.

structured_extraction.program_description: A 12-week, paid, in-person leadership course designed to help residents and local leaders build skills in community development, violence prevention, environmental design, and neighborhood improvement. Participants gain practical experience in community leadership and organizing, storytelling, grant writing, project planning, and data-informed problem solving. The program supports participants in designing and implementing grant-funded neighborhood improvement projects within their own communities.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: The program provides paid participation in a 12-week in-person leadership course. Participants gain hands-on training in community leadership, environmental design, public safety strategy, violence prevention, storytelling, grant writing, project planning, and data-informed problem solving. Throughout the program, participants have the opportunity to design and implement grant-funded neighborhood improvement projects within their own communities.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Aspiring community leaders, emerging leaders, and small business owners in Baltimore's Northern District who are passionate about community change and committed to turning ideas into action.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Participants design and implement grant-funded neighborhood improvement projects within their own communities. Training covers community development, violence prevention, environmental design, and neighborhood improvement initiatives.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Applicants must be located in Baltimore's Northern District.
requirements_list: Located in Baltimore's Northern District
Interested in community development, violence prevention, and neighborhood improvement
Aspiring community leader or emerging leader
Ready to deepen impact and take active role in shaping neighborhood
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Interested applicants can learn more about the program through virtual or in-person information sessions held in April. They can then apply online through an Office Form. The application window closes on May 3, 2026. Program sessions run from May 18, 2026, through August 7, 2026.

structured_extraction.program_description: A competitive awards program that provides capital funds and operating funds to support locally driven community development work and neighborhood revitalization efforts in historically disinvested areas.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Up to $1,020,000 in operating funds available through Round 6. The program provides capital funds and operating funds for community-driven revitalization initiatives.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Community development corporations, neighborhood-based development organizations, umbrella organizations and other neighborhood-based organizations working in historically disinvested areas.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Community-driven revitalization initiatives and neighborhood revitalization and transformation efforts.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Historically disinvested areas in Baltimore City.
requirements_list: Eligible organizations include community development corporations, neighborhood-based development organizations, umbrella organizations and other neighborhood-based organizations
Projects must support locally-driven revitalization initiatives
Applicants must meet full eligibility requirements outlined in the Notice of Funds Available (NOFA)
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Submit applications through the online portal. Applications opened March 23, 2026 and are due by April 24, 2026 at 5:00 PM ET. Review the NOFA guidelines carefully for full eligibility requirements and application guidelines.

structured_extraction.program_description: A federal program from HUD that helps Baltimore City distribute federal funds directly to non-profit and public agencies supporting housing and public-service programs. The program funds 26 different types of activities, with at least 70% of funds directly benefiting low- and moderate-income people. The main goal is to develop viable communities by providing safe, affordable homes for low- and middle-income families and creating more local job opportunities through community development initiatives.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Federal grants allocated through an annual funding process. Funds support 26 types of activities including housing, public services, and economic development. At least 70% of funds must directly benefit low- and moderate-income people. Applications and reports are submitted through Neighborly software.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Non-profit organizations and public agencies working on housing and public services in Baltimore City, as well as low- and middle-income families and community organizations.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Affordable housing for families with low to moderate incomes, public services, economic development, slum prevention and remediation, and urgent community needs.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Program serves Baltimore City only.
requirements_list: Project must meet at least one goal: help people with low or moderate incomes, prevent or fix slums or blighted areas, or address an urgent need
At least 70% of funds must directly benefit low- and moderate-income people
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Non-profit organizations and governmental entities submit Requests for Funding through an annual Request for Proposals process managed by the Consolidated Planning Division. Applications are submitted through Neighborly software. DHCD monitors recipient performance and activities to ensure CDBG Program compliance.

structured_extraction.program_description: A free training program that educates volunteers on how to prepare for hazards and cope with emergencies. The program covers basic disaster prevention, preparation, and response skills including fire safety, light search and rescue, team organization, communications, and emergency medical procedures. Trained members can volunteer with the Baltimore City Office of Emergency Management to support outreach, emergency response, and recovery operations.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Free training program. Participants must complete a FEMA SID registration, enroll in and complete an in-person CERT training course (which includes two FEMA online courses: Incident Command System IS-315.a and Introduction to Community Emergency Response Team IS-317.a), and support one OEM-sponsored preparedness and outreach event per year. Training consists of a 2-day course with 8 hours per day. Trained members meet quarterly throughout the year for additional trainings and informational sessions available in both in-person and hybrid formats.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Individuals who live or work in Baltimore City and are at least 18 years of age who want to learn emergency response skills and volunteer in their community.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Training and preparation to help keep yourself, your family, and your community safe before, during, and after a disaster. Trained members can assist others in their family, neighborhood, and community until first responders arrive, volunteer during large local events, and help during emergencies.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available to residents and employees of Baltimore City only. Participants must live or work in Baltimore City.
requirements_list: Must be at least 18 years of age
Must live or work in Baltimore City
Must register for a FEMA SID
Must enroll in and complete an in-person CERT training course
Must complete two FEMA online courses: Incident Command System (IS-315.a) and Introduction to Community Emergency Response Team (IS-317.a)
Must support one OEM-sponsored preparedness and outreach event per year
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Interested individuals register for a FEMA SID, then enroll in an in-person CERT training course through one of the scheduled training opportunities listed on the website. Training consists of a 2-day course with 8 hours of instruction per day. After completing the course, members must support one OEM-sponsored preparedness and outreach event per year.

structured_extraction.program_name: Community Land Trusts - Homeownership & Rental NOFAs
structured_extraction.program_description: The Baltimore City Department of Housing & Community Development issued two Notices of Funding Availability for the Affordable Housing Trust Fund Community Land Trusts Program to support both homeownership and rental projects sponsored by Community Land Trusts. The rental component makes up to $1.5 million available to support new construction and/or preservation of existing rentals under community land trust terms, where the developer owns physical improvements and the CLT owns land under a 99-year affordable housing ground lease. The homeownership component makes up to $4.0 million available to support perpetually affordable homeownership through a shared equity model where land is owned by the CLT. The program promotes equitable community development by directing funds to communities suffering from historical disinvestment and integrating land trust housing as part of mixed-income housing strategies.
eligible_industries: Real Estate and Rental and Leasing
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Rental component: Up to $750,000 per project maximum. Funds can support up to 50% of Total Development Cost (TDC) for units restricted to 50% AMI, or up to 66% of TDC for units restricted to 30% AMI. Maximum per unit: $20,000 (fewer than 10 units) or $50,000 (10+ units) for 50% AMI households; $100,000 per unit for 30% AMI households. Homeownership component: Up to $1,000,000 per project maximum. Funds can support up to 50% of TDC for units at ≤50% AMI or up to 66% TDC for units at ≤30% AMI. Maximum $50,000 per unit for ≤50% AMI; $100,000 per unit for ≤30% AMI. Up to 25% advancement for predevelopment/acquisition and up to 20% of award for operating costs directly related to project implementation.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Community Land Trusts organized or managed by nonprofit organizations exempt from taxation under §501(c)(2), (3), or (4) of the US Internal Revenue Code, and registered as Affordable Housing Land Trusts with Maryland Department of Assessments and Taxation. CLTs must partner with experienced developers (completed at least 5 development projects).
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Land acquisition and site control, project development and construction, personnel and consultant fees, environmental sustainability initiatives, local hiring and apprenticeship programs, architecture and engineering costs, marketing and sales activities, community engagement activities, and operating costs directly related to project implementation.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City neighborhoods, with focus on historically disinvested areas. Projects must demonstrate consistency with community/neighborhood revitalization plans and leverage additional investment with local residents and stakeholders leading revitalization efforts.
requirements_list: Community Land Trust sponsorship required and registered as Affordable Housing Land Trust with Maryland Department of Assessments and Taxation
Must be nonprofit organization exempt from taxation under §501(c)(2), (3), or (4) of the US Internal Revenue Code or demonstrate nonprofit management
Must partner with experienced developer (completed at least 5 development projects)
Site plan (conceptual acceptable) showing location, amenities, sustainability features, current parks/green spaces
Personnel budget and consultant list if requesting funds for personnel/consultants
Site control at submission; title within 12 months of Funding Agreement execution
Management plan with experienced management company and current project references
Resumes/qualification statements of applicant and principal development team members
Comprehensive development budget with all funding sources and status
Letters of interest/commitment from all participating funding sources
Construction budget must include builder profit, overhead, prevailing wages, and management
Projects must be completed within 2 years of funding agreement execution
Demonstrate capacity and community representation (at least 1/3 of board should be community members)
Market data supporting need for permanent affordability
Must comply with Section 14 of the Annotated Code of Maryland Real Property Article
Meet all zoning and development requirements; obtain necessary variances
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Prospective applicants must participate in a pre-development meeting. Applications accepted through September 2, 2022 for both rental and homeownership NOFAs. Submissions can be made online through AHTF website or via email to DHCD.AHTFNOFA@baltimorecity.gov. Funding is provided on a reimbursement basis post-Board of Estimates approval. Awards announced pending Board of Estimates approval.

structured_extraction.program_name: Community Land Trusts - Operating Costs NOFA
structured_extraction.program_description: Funding from the Affordable Housing Trust Fund to support Community Land Trust (CLT) operating costs. Up to $500,000 available total; applicants can request up to $100,000 per CLT entity. Supports operating, personnel, and predevelopment costs for CLTs creating affordable housing to low and very low income households in Baltimore City.
eligible_industries: Grocery Stores and Fresh Food Retailers
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Up to $500,000 available from the Affordable Housing Trust Fund with applicants able to request up to $100,000 per CLT entity. Funding supports operating, personnel, and predevelopment costs including market and feasibility analysis, carrying costs, financing fees, legal fees, project management staff, and general organizational operating costs such as rent, utilities, salaries, and supplies.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Community Land Trusts with 2 or more years of operation and 5 or more affordable units built or in process providing affordable housing in Baltimore City
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Market and Financial Feasibility Analysis, Carrying Costs, Financing and Lender Fees, Legal Fees for closing and financing, Project management staff, General organizational operating costs including rent, utilities, salaries, and supplies
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City only
requirements_list: Must be a Community Land Trust organization
Must be organized or managed by nonprofit exempt from taxation under § 501(c)(2), (3), or (4) of the Internal Revenue Code or demonstrate legal organization and management by a nonprofit
Must have 2 or more years of operation
Must have 5 or more affordable units built or in process
Must provide affordable housing to low and very low income households in Baltimore City
Must be registered as an Affordable Housing Land Trust with Maryland
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Applications accepted through October 6, 2023 at 4:00 PM EST. Awards announced pending Board of Estimates approval.

structured_extraction.program_description: Provides one-on-one peer support, outreach, and linkages to services. All calls are answered 24/7 by Maryland Certified Peer Recovery Specialists who provide care linkages and follow-ups to resources and supports.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: One-on-one peer support and outreach provided 24/7 by Maryland Certified Peer Recovery Specialists, including care linkages and follow-ups to resources and supports for individuals seeking assistance.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Individuals in Baltimore City seeking peer recovery support and assistance connecting to services.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Peer support, outreach, and linkages to recovery resources and services.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City.
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Call the Community Peer Project to connect with a Maryland Certified Peer Recovery Specialist who provides 24/7 support.

structured_extraction.program_description: The Baltimore City Department of Transportation Community-Based Programs support community groups in creating fun and creative public space improvement projects in neighborhoods. The Community-Led Placemaking Program specifically enables community groups to design and implement projects in public spaces like streets, sidewalks, and alleys to enhance neighborhood aesthetics, help slow down traffic, and provide more space for walking and gathering. Project types include artistic painting, landscape plantings, planters and barriers for traffic calming, signage, parklets, and special urban design projects. The applicant community group is responsible for funding and implementing the project, while DOT provides design guidance, regulatory approval, and technical support.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: The program provides technical assistance and regulatory approval for community groups to design and implement placemaking projects in public spaces. Project types include paint in the right-of-way, landscape plantings, planters and barriers, signage, parklets, and special projects. The applicant community group must pay for and implement the project; DOT provides design guidance, approval, and technical support.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Community groups, neighborhood associations, local businesses, nonprofits, school parent groups, and residents in Baltimore City who want to create public space improvement projects.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: The program supports the design, approval, and implementation of community-led placemaking projects including artistic painting on streets or sidewalks, landscape plantings, planters and barriers for traffic calming, welcome signs, parklets, temporary public spaces, art installations, special lighting, and other urban design projects.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: The program is available to all Baltimore City neighborhoods.
requirements_list: Design rendering must be submitted
Location(s) of project must be specified
Materials to be used must be listed

Letters of support or signed petitions from adjacent occupants required (60% of block occupants for parklet and mid-block projects; 60% of occupants of three properties in each direction for intersections)
Proof of property owner support from property(s) directly abutting the project
Proof that organization is in good standing with State of Maryland
Commercial liability insurance ($1 million for each occurrence, $2 million in aggregate) required for parklets and special projects
Maintenance plan for the project
Projects cannot contain obscene, vulgar, or violent messages
Projects cannot block walkways or violate ADA requirements
Projects cannot introduce roadway safety hazards
Projects cannot require unreasonable maintenance by DOT
Projects cannot cause damage to DOT assets or utilities
Projects cannot contain harmful or poisonous plants
Paint must be pre-approved by DOT (specific brands allowed)
Designs cannot incorporate words or political messages for paint projects
For traffic calming elements, must either submit request to 311 or hire contractor with approved plans before submitting placemaking application
All designs, materials, and locations subject to DOT approval
Applicant group responsible for maintenance and safety
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Submit project designs and documents through the Community-Based Programs Application. For projects including traffic calming elements, first submit a traffic calming request to 311 or hire a contractor to install traffic calming elements with DOT approval. Upon approval, receive a written agreement explaining what has been approved, project timeline, maintenance responsibilities, and special rules to follow.

structured_extraction.program_description: A professional fellowship program that provides training and experience in government accounting, auditing, and financial management through the City Comptroller's office.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Professional fellowship providing training and work experience in government financial management, accounting, and auditing through placement in the Baltimore City Comptroller's office.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Individuals interested in professional training and experience in government accounting and financial management.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Training and professional development in accounting, auditing, and financial management for fellows placed in the Comptroller's office.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City, Maryland
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Application submission through the provided form at the specified URL.

structured_extraction.program_name: Computer Training - Enoch Pratt Free Library
structured_extraction.program_description: Free computer classes offered in person at local library branches where participants learn to use computers, write resumes, and use Microsoft Office or Google tools.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Free in-person computer classes covering basic computer use, resume writing, and Microsoft Office or Google tools applications.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Baltimore City residents seeking to build computer skills.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Educational training in computer basics, resume writing, and office software.

structured_extraction.program_description: A competitive grant opportunity administered by Baltimore City's Mayor's Office of Homeless Services for qualified nonprofit organizations and government agencies to provide services to individuals and families who are at-risk of homelessness, currently homeless, or living with HIV or AIDS. Organizations submit one application to be considered for multiple eligible funding sources. The program draws funding from six sources: HUD Emergency Solutions Grant (ESG), State of Maryland Homeless Solutions Program, Baltimore City Department of Social Services, HUD Housing Opportunities for Persons with AIDS/HIV (HOPWA), Maryland Department of Health State Special Funds, and Baltimore City General Funds. Programs receive annual funding for a performance period typically from July 1 through June 30. Eligible service categories include emergency shelter, drop-in services/day centers, transitional housing, rapid re-housing, permanent supportive housing, street outreach, eviction prevention, housing stabilization and homelessness prevention, and HIV-AIDS services.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Competitive grants drawn from six funding sources: HUD Emergency Solutions Grant (ESG), State of Maryland Homeless Solutions Program, Baltimore City Department of Social Services, HUD Housing Opportunities for Persons with AIDS/HIV (HOPWA), Maryland Department of Health State Special Funds, and Baltimore City General Funds. Programs receive annual funding for a performance period typically from July 1 through June 30. Eligible service categories include emergency shelter, drop-in services/day centers, transitional housing, rapid re-housing, permanent supportive housing, street outreach, eviction prevention, housing stabilization and homelessness prevention, and HIV-AIDS services.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Qualified nonprofit organizations and government agencies providing services to individuals and families who are at-risk of homelessness, currently homeless, or living with HIV or AIDS in Baltimore City.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Funding for programs serving individuals and families who are at-risk of homelessness, currently homeless, or living with HIV or AIDS. Eligible uses include emergency shelter, drop-in services/day centers, transitional housing, rapid re-housing, permanent supportive housing, street outreach, eviction prevention, housing stabilization and homelessness prevention, and HIV-AIDS services.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City only. The performance period runs from July 1 through June 30 (City Fiscal Year).

structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Organizations submit one Consolidated Funding Application with project proposal to be considered for multiple eligible funding sources. Organizations must create an account and log into the Neighborly portal before the deadline and add two points of contact. An authorized individual at the agency uploads all application materials to the Neighborly platform. The application questions differ for new and renewal applicants. After completing the application, the authorized individual certifies and submits it electronically. Neighborly sends an automated message confirming receipt. A bidder's conference webinar is recommended for all applicants. The typical application timeline includes: release of RFP, bidder's conference webinar, application submission deadline, application review period (including threshold/eligibility review and panel evaluation), conditional award notification, contract development period, and contract commencement on July 1. Application templates and budget templates are provided based on service category.

structured_extraction.program_description: A competitive grant opportunity administered by the Mayor's Office of Homeless Services through which non-profit organizations can submit one application to be considered for multiple eligible funding sources to provide services to individuals and families who are at-risk of homelessness, currently homeless, low-income and living with HIV or AIDS, or at risk of crises including those with behavioral health needs. Funds a full spectrum of housing and services including eviction prevention, day centers, emergency shelter, transitional housing, comprehensive street outreach services, rapid rehousing, permanent supportive housing, and housing/services for people living with HIV or AIDS.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Competitive grants funded through multiple sources including the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development Emergency Solutions Grant (ESG), State of Maryland Homeless Solutions Program (HSP), Baltimore City Department of Social Services (DSS), U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development Housing Opportunities for Persons with AIDS/HIV (HOPWA), Baltimore City Opioid Restitution Fund, and Baltimore City General Funds. Funding amounts include ESG (~$1.85M), HSP (~$2.97M), DSS (~$314K-$500K), HOPWA (~$200K for Baltimore City), Opioid Restitution Fund (TBD), and General Funds ($9M). Eligible project types and service categories include transitional housing, street outreach, rapid re-housing, permanent supportive housing, housing stabilization and homelessness prevention, housing and services for people with HIV/AIDS, emergency shelter, comprehensive street outreach, eviction prevention, and day centers.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Non-profit organizations providing services to individuals and families who are at-risk of homelessness, currently homeless, low-income and living with HIV or AIDS, or at risk of crises including those with behavioral health needs. Specific populations served include individuals experiencing literal homelessness, families with children experiencing homelessness, unaccompanied youth under 25, individuals at imminent risk of homelessness, individuals and families fleeing domestic violence, at-risk individuals and families with annual income below 30% AMI, and individuals with behavioral health needs.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Funding supports services in the following categories: transitional housing, street outreach, rapid re-housing, permanent supportive housing, housing stabilization and homelessness prevention, housing and services for people with HIV/AIDS, emergency shelter, comprehensive street outreach, eviction prevention, day centers, outreach and engagement services, case management and support services, emergency health services, housing identification and placement, rental and financial assistance, transportation, meals, shelter operations and facility management, staff training, supplies, health and wellness support, and clothing and hygiene products.

Applications can also be submitted as Word documents aligned with Appendix A Scope of Work. After submission, applications undergo threshold and eligibility review followed by panel evaluation. Conditional awards are announced in April 2025, contract development begins in May 2025, and the grant term begins July 1, 2025.

structured_extraction.program_description: A federal funding opportunity administered by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) that seeks to address and reduce homelessness by adding new units of permanent supportive housing through new construction, acquisition, or rehabilitation. The program provides one-time CoC Builds awards to qualified collaborative applicants selected through a competitive request for proposals process. Approximately $175 million in total funding is available nationally, with approximately $110 million reserved for Continua of Care in states with populations over 2.5 million people, including Maryland and Baltimore City.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Approximately $175 million in total funding is made available nationally to add new permanent supportive housing units through new construction, acquisition, or rehabilitation. Of this total, approximately $110 million is reserved for Continua of Care in states with populations over 2.5 million people, including Baltimore City. One-time CoC Builds awards are provided to support permanent supportive housing. Up to 20% of funds can support rental assistance, case management, and supportive services. Up to 10% can be used for project administrative costs. The selected applicant is expected to provide both supportive services and property management services. Projects must include a developer, property manager, and service provider either through memoranda of understanding between organizations or within the same organization.
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: Friday, October 18, 2024 at 3:00 pm EST (local Baltimore RFP); Thursday, November 21, 2024 at 11:59:59 p.m. (HUD submission deadline)
structured_extraction.program_audience: CoC-designated Collaborative Applicants to serve the Baltimore City Continuum of Care (MD-501). Only one application may be submitted by the CoC-designated Collaborative Applicant. Program serves individuals and families experiencing homelessness where at least one household member has a disability, including chronically homeless individuals, seniors, veterans, families with children, youth (18-24), persons with disabilities, mental illness, substance use disorder, domestic violence survivors, and persons with HIV/AIDS.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Adding new units of permanent supportive housing through new construction, acquisition, or rehabilitation. Funds support project-based rental assistance, supportive services (case management, mental health services, substance use treatment, healthcare), operating costs (maintenance, repairs, utilities, property tax, insurance), and project administrative costs. Up to 20% of award for supportive services, operating costs, and project-based rental assistance. Up to 10% for project administrative costs.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: The program is administered by the City of Baltimore for the Baltimore City Continuum of Care (MD-501) and serves Baltimore City only. Projects must be consistent with the City of Baltimore's 2021-2025 Consolidated Plan, focusing on Affordable Housing and Housing for Special Needs Populations.

structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Organizations must submit one PDF electronic copy of the proposal and all required supporting documents to BaltimorePSH@lesardevelopment.com by the deadline. Complete application narrative per format specifications (25 pages maximum, double-spaced, 12-point Times Roman, 1-inch margins). Submit funding request and match tables, match commitment letters with documentation, and for in-kind services submit partner agency commitment letter. Submit approved indirect cost rate or cost allocation plan if applicable. Proposals are evaluated and scored internally, then reviewed by a selection panel with potential interviews. The Resource Allocation Committee reviews and scores proposals with recommendations to the CoC Board. The CoC Board approves the final recommendation, and the selected applicant receives notification. The selected applicant's application is then submitted to HUD via grants.gov by the specified deadline. MOHS may request additional clarification information; verbal inquiries must be provided in writing.

structured_extraction.program_description: Coordinated Access Navigator Sites serve as entry points for individuals and families currently experiencing homelessness to assess eligibility for housing programs and receive assistance with gathering necessary information to complete housing applications. Coordinated Access Navigators help determine if individuals qualify for various housing assistance programs tailored to specific populations and provide support throughout the application process.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Free assessment, eligibility determination, and application assistance for housing programs. Navigator sites provide intake services to identify which housing assistance programs individuals and families qualify for based on their circumstances (homelessness status, age, veteran status, HIV/AIDS diagnosis, etc.) and assist with gathering information and preparing housing applications.

structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Assessment, eligibility determination, and housing application assistance for housing programs

requirements_list: Currently experiencing homelessness
Reside in Baltimore City
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Contact the appropriate Coordinated Access Navigator Site by phone to schedule an appointment or find a Navigator through the Coordinated Access System page. Sites serve different populations: People Encouraging People (general population), Springboard Community Services (youth ages 18-24), MOHS HOPWA Program (people with HIV/AIDS), New Vision House of Hope (veterans), or The Baltimore Station (veterans). Alternatively, walk in during business hours at Health Care for the Homeless, Paul's Place, Beans and Bread, or Springboard Community Services.

Employees receive secure identification cards recognized by the Baltimore Police Department, enabling them to enter restricted areas during disasters to assess damage, maintain IT systems, meet regulatory obligations, and secure vital records.

Must have critical employees who need access to facilities during emergencies
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Businesses can enroll through the CEAS program to have their critical employees credentialed and issued secure identification cards. Contact www.ceas.com for more information on enrollment.

structured_extraction.program_description: The City of Baltimore provides capital support to cultural organizations every two years through General Obligation bonds to fund eligible capital improvements to their facilities. The program aims to support organizations that promote arts and culture in Baltimore City and contribute to the City's unique identity.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Organizations can apply for General Obligation bonds for capital improvements on a reimbursement basis. Total funding available is $1 million per year. Individual awards do not exceed $200,000 over two years, with typical awards between $50,000-$100,000 over a two-year period. Funds support building systems improvements, public access improvements, renovations, and expansions.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Non-profit museums, galleries, theaters, and other arts or cultural venues located in Baltimore City, including those within designated arts and entertainment districts.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Capital improvements to facilities with a minimum 15-year service life, including building systems upgrades (elevators, roofs, HVAC, windows), plaza or entrance upgrades for accessibility, exterior and interior renovations, fire protection improvements, ADA and accessibility improvements, and museum or exhibit expansions. Projects must cost at least $50,000 and cannot be emergency repairs or maintenance.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Organizations must have a physical location in Baltimore City. The facility must be open to the general public. Museums, galleries, and theaters throughout the City are eligible. Other types of arts or cultural venues located within designated arts and entertainment districts may also apply.

Projects cannot exceed $200,000

structured_extraction.program_description: An employer-driven training program designed to provide job seekers with little or no skills in a specific industry with targeted training, while helping businesses obtain and hire skilled workers for hard-to-fill or newly created positions. MOED reimburses businesses up to 50 percent of training costs to develop a more productive and efficient workforce. Training can include wages, tools, uniforms, and training courses, provided by the employer or through WIOA eligible training providers.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: MOED reimburses businesses up to 50 percent of training costs, which may include wages, tools, uniforms, and training courses. Training can be provided by the employer or through WIOA eligible training providers. Trainees must be hired into full-time permanent positions with wages of $10 per hour or higher. MOED provides marketing, recruitment, and pre-screening of applicants. Industry-specific training is available for job seekers with little or no skills.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Job seekers with little or no skills in target industries, and for-profit businesses of all industries in Baltimore City that need to train new hires for hard-to-fill positions
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Training costs including wages, tools, uniforms, and training courses for new employees; industry-specific job training and worker recruitment

Training can be provided by employer or through WIOA eligible training providers
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Complete the Customized Training/OJT Business Application. MOED provides marketing, recruitment, and pre-screening of applicants.

Targets formerly vacant homes with Vacant Building Notices (VBN) in designated Impact Investment Areas or Middle Neighborhoods. Funding available for total development costs.

structured_extraction.program_description: The Digital Equity Fund supports community-led digital inclusion initiatives and provides grants to Baltimore-based nonprofit organizations working in close partnership with communities to address the digital divide. The fund invests in projects across three grant tiers to help address gaps in digital literacy and skills, targeting vulnerable residents who lack access to digital devices and internet connectivity. Three types of grants are offered: Tier 1 (Education and Outreach) up to $200,000 for digital literacy education training; Tier 2 (Planning and Advanced Digital Education) up to $200,000 for IT fundamentals programming leading to industry-recognized certifications; Tier 3 (Implementation and Digital Creatives) up to $200,000 for digital creatives and virtual makerspaces programming at local recreation centers.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Three grant tiers are available: Tier 1 provides up to $200,000 for digital literacy education training, including sub-tiers for older adults and broader community tech hubs; Tier 2 provides up to $200,000 for advanced digital education and IT fundamentals programming leading to industry-recognized certifications (such as Cisco ITE, A+, CompTIA ITF+, Net+, Security+); Tier 3 provides up to $200,000 for digital creatives and virtual makerspaces programming, including coding, digital media creation, robotics, video editing, and 3D printing at local recreation centers.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Baltimore-based 501(c)(3) nonprofit organizations serving Baltimore residents, particularly those serving groups most likely to be left behind in the digital age including people with disabilities, older adults, racial and ethnic minorities, immigrants, non-English speakers, returning citizens, LGBTQIA+ youth, and people experiencing homelessness.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Funding can be used for digital literacy education training, IT fundamentals skills training and certification programs, digital creatives and virtual makerspaces programming at recreation centers, and community-based activities to raise awareness of the digital divide. Specific skills areas include computer basics, internet use, digital skills for job seekers, industry-recognized IT certifications, coding, digital media creation, robotics, video editing, 3D printing, and capacity building for neighborhood digital inclusion planning and implementation.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: The program is limited to Baltimore City. Applicants must be Baltimore-based 501(c)(3) nonprofit organizations and grantees must serve Baltimore residents.
requirements_list: Applicant must be a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization
Organization must be based in Baltimore City
Organization must serve Baltimore residents
Must work in close partnership with communities
Applicants must plan to address the needs of groups most likely to be left behind in the digital age
Organizations can submit a grant proposal for each grant type

Information sessions were held to help potential applicants prepare their proposals. Past session materials including slide decks and video recordings are available for reference. Questions not covered in the Request for Applications can be directed to the email contact.

structured_extraction.program_description: A joint effort between the Maryland Department of Health and the Baltimore City Fire Department that enables first responders to leave naloxone with patients and their support systems during overdose-related 911 calls in Baltimore City. This ensures life-saving naloxone resources are available to those most likely to use it in emergencies, regardless of whether the patient goes to the hospital.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Free naloxone left with patients and their support systems by first responders during overdose-related 911 emergency calls. First responders distribute naloxone kits directly at no cost to recipients.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Baltimore City residents who experience opioid overdoses and respond to 911 emergency calls, as well as their support systems.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Naloxone distribution during emergency overdose response to patients and their support systems.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City only
requirements_list: Experience an overdose-related 911 call in Baltimore City
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: The program is activated automatically when first responders respond to overdose-related 911 calls in Baltimore City. No application required—naloxone is provided by EMS during overdose emergency calls.

structured_extraction.program_description: A federally funded congregate nutrition program established under the Older Americans Act that provides free nutritious meals in a friendly social atmosphere for seniors 60 and older at over 50 congregate dining sites and 10 senior centers throughout Baltimore City. The program promotes health, reduces isolation, and offers opportunities for socializing, education, and activities. Participants may also reside in certain older adult housing. Meals include Kosher and Korean meal options, with optional suggested donations at $1.25 for regular meals and $2.00 for Kosher meals.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Participants receive free nutritious lunches or dinner meals (including Kosher and Korean meal options) at over 50 congregate dining sites and 10 senior centers throughout Baltimore City. Meals are provided at various times throughout the week. Donations are optional and suggested at $1.25 for regular meals and $2.00 for Kosher meals.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Seniors 60 years of age or older, their spouses regardless of age, disabled persons younger than 60 who reside in residential buildings where the program operates, and residents of certain older adult housing in Baltimore City.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Meals must be consumed at Eating Together congregate dining sites and senior centers; funds support the provision of nutritious lunches or dinners.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Program operates at over 50 congregate dining sites and 10 senior centers throughout Baltimore City. Participants must be able to attend a meal program at a site in their residential building or nearby location.

Must be a Baltimore City resident or resident of participating older adult housing
Must complete a registration form to participate
Menus are posted monthly; participants can reserve meals on preferred dates
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Call 443-573-0161 to sign up and register for the program. Complete a registration form to become an eligible participant. Receive a membership card to swipe at each meal attendance. Review monthly menus and reserve meals on preferred dates. Visit one of the Eating Together sites (50+ congregate dining sites or 10 senior centers) in Baltimore City for meals.

structured_extraction.program_description: A competitive grant program administered by the Mayor's Office of Homeless Services to provide emergency shelter services for persons experiencing homelessness in Baltimore City. The program funds the operation of three emergency homeless shelter sites that serve as dignified residential settings supporting individuals to transition to housing stability. Services include 24/7 shelter, case management, housing stabilization planning, and coordinated access to permanent housing, following the City's Continuum of Care Action Plan with the goal of making homelessness rare, brief, and nonrecurring.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Competitive grant funding for operating emergency homeless shelter sites. Organizations receiving awards operate shelter sites for single men, single women, families, or combinations thereof. Specific sites include Pinderhughes Homeless Shelter (1200 N. Fremont Ave.) with 70 single adult female beds and 8 family beds, and Weinberg Housing & Resource Center (620 Fallsway) with 175 single adult male beds and 75 single adult female female beds. Funding supports day-to-day operations, case management, complaint response, data collection, linkage to community support, and supportive services. Services include meals (twice daily, 365 days/year), shelter monitoring and security, facility maintenance, fire safety compliance, and staff training in trauma-informed care, harm reduction, racial equity, and LGBTQ cultural competency. Performance period was July 1, 2020 through June 30, 2021. Funding comes from a combination of federal, state, and local appropriations.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Registered non-profit 501(c) tax-exempt organizations and city agencies operating emergency homeless shelter services; persons experiencing homelessness in Baltimore City
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Operating emergency homeless shelter sites that provide dignified residential settings and services to support persons experiencing homelessness to transition to housing stability. Funds cover management of day-to-day shelter operations (maintenance, food services, janitorial, monitoring), case management services, complaint response and monitoring, data collection and entry, linkage and connection to community support, meals and food service, shelter monitoring and security personnel, facility maintenance and operations, fire safety equipment and inspections, customer satisfaction surveys, staff training in trauma-informed care and harm reduction, waste management and pest control.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City

structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Organizations submit a proposal including completed Emergency Shelter Application form, Request for Proposal response, Budget Proposal Template, work plan using modified logic model template, staffing plan with position details and required credentials, and conflict of interest questionnaire. structured_extraction.program_description: Federal emergency funding allocated through the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security Act (CARES Act), Public Law 116-136, and administered by HUD to prevent, prepare for, and respond to the coronavirus pandemic among individuals and families experiencing homelessness or receiving homeless assistance in Baltimore City. The City of Baltimore received $6,571,738.00 in total ESG-CV funds. More than two-thirds of the $15.7 million allocation ($10.7 million) supports rapid rehousing and homelessness prevention. Remaining funds support emergency shelter operations, street outreach, data management (HMIS), emergency supplies such as personal protective equipment and cleaning supplies, medical expenses, increased food costs, and program administration and oversight. Funds are distributed to Continuum of Care service providers.

Of the $6,571,738.00 allocation, $657,173.80 is designated for administration activities including general management, oversight, coordination, and reporting. Remaining funds are distributed to Continuum of Care providers for project activities including rapid rehousing ($10.7 million), homelessness prevention, emergency shelter operations, street outreach, HMIS, eviction prevention, and COVID-19 response activities. Funds may be used for expanding project capacity, emergency supplies such as personal protective equipment and cleaning supplies, medical expenses, and increased food costs.

structured_extraction.program_name: Expedited Reimbursement Program for Sewage Backups
structured_extraction.program_description: The Baltimore City Department of Public Works administers a reimbursement program for sewage backups caused by capacity-related wet weather events. The program offers up to $5,000 per dwelling unit per event to cover reasonable, documented cleanup, disinfection, and disposal service costs. Eligible expenses include cleanup and disinfection costs resulting from sewage backups, and insurance deductibles may be reimbursable if demonstrably linked to cleanup and disinfection activities. Reimbursement is limited to $5,000 per dwelling, per occurrence.

Applicants must obtain a final written determination from their insurance company before processing.

structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Apply online or submit a completed application by email, certified mail, or commercial delivery to the Baltimore City Department of Public Works Bureau of Water and Wastewater within 90 days of the incident. structured_extraction.program_name: FY 2025 Continuum of Care (CoC) Program Competition
structured_extraction.program_description: Federal funding program administered by HUD and locally by the Baltimore City Mayor's Office of Homeless Services (MOHS) that provides competitive grants to support homeless services. The program promotes a community-wide commitment to ending homelessness by providing funding to nonprofit providers and state and local governments to quickly rehouse individuals and families experiencing homelessness while minimizing the impacts of trauma and dislocation. Funds support permanent housing, supportive services, Homeless Management Information Systems, and access to mainstream programs to optimize self-sufficiency. The program uses a person-centered, data-driven approach to make homelessness rare, brief, and nonrecurring. In Baltimore City, over 75 percent of CoC funding is directed to Permanent Supportive Housing programs combining long-term housing subsidies with supportive services for chronically homeless individuals. Applicants can apply for new projects, expansion projects, renewal projects, or Youth Homeless Demonstration Program (YHDP) renewal or replacement projects.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Competitive Federal grants available annually through HUD for multiple project types: Permanent Supportive Housing (PSH), Rapid Rehousing (RRH), Transitional Housing (TH), Joint TH-RRH, Safe Haven (SH), and Supportive Services Only (SSO) including street outreach and coordinated entry. FY 2025 total available funding is $42,797,644, comprised of $31,796,073 in Annual Renewal Demand (ARD), $6,359,215 in CoC Bonus Project Funding, $3,142,356 in Domestic Violence Bonus Project Funding, and $1,500,000 in CoC Planning Grant Funds. Funding provided to nonprofit providers and state and local governments to support rapid rehousing, trauma-informed services, dislocation prevention, housing subsidies, leasing, rental assistance, supportive services, operations, HMIS participation, and mainstream program access for individuals and families experiencing homelessness. Specific grant amounts and project types are determined through the local competition process. In Baltimore City, over 75 percent of CoC funding is directed to Permanent Supportive Housing programs combining long-term housing subsidies with supportive services for chronically homeless individuals. There is a 30% funding cap on permanent housing ($9.5 million for Baltimore City).

structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Permanent housing programs, supportive services, Homeless Management Information Systems, rapid rehousing, trauma-informed services, dislocation prevention, housing subsidies, leasing, rental assistance, case management, employment assistance, mental health services, substance abuse treatment, legal services, food assistance, transportation, utility deposits, housing search counseling, street outreach services, emergency shelter operations, transitional housing, safe haven operations, landlord recruitment and incentive programs, move-in assistance, security deposits (up to 2 months rent), housing start-up expenses, utility assistance (arrears up to 6 months; up to 3 months prospective), rental arrears payment (up to 6 months, one-time), moving expenses, legal fees, cellular phone/internet provision, and access to mainstream programs and self-sufficiency support for individuals and families experiencing homelessness. structured_extraction.application_process_overview: HUD releases Notice of Funding Availability (NOFA) annually. Local Baltimore City hosts competition for 60 to 75 days. Applicants create an account in the Neighborly portal, log in, and add two points of contact for their organization. An authorized individual at the agency uploads all application materials and supporting documentation. The authorized individual then certifies and submits the application via Neighborly. Applicants can choose to apply for new projects, expansion projects, renewal projects, or Youth Homeless Demonstration Program (YHDP) renewal or replacement projects using the appropriate application template. Applications are reviewed by the Resource Allocation Committee, projects are ranked, and notifications of acceptance or rejection are sent to applicants. The final consolidated CoC application is submitted to HUD.
